docs.title: Technical Overview
docs.text:
The utils.crawl_local_files module provides local filesystem traversal and content extraction capabilities for the Codebase-Knowledge-Builder system. It serves as an alternative to utils.crawl_github_files, exposing a compatible return interface ({"files": {filepath: content}}) when operating directly against a local workspace or repository instead of fetching data via the GitHub REST API.

The module performs a single-pass traversal using os.walk, incorporating: - Rule-based directory pruning to eliminate unnecessary branches early. - .gitignore compatibility using pathspec.PathSpec (gitwildmatch syntax). - User-supplied glob inclusion and exclusion matching via fnmatch. - Maximum file size thresholds to prevent loading large binaries or assets. - UTF-8 text decoding with fallback detection to skip non-text or binary files safely. - Real-time ANSI-colored logging and crawl metrics reporting.

flowchart TD
    Start([Start Crawl]) --> CheckDir{os.path.isdir?}
    CheckDir -- No --> RaiseErr[Raise ValueError]
    CheckDir -- Yes --> LoadGitignore[Load .gitignore if present]

    LoadGitignore --> WalkDirs[os.walk directory]

    subgraph DirFiltering[Directory Level Filter]
        WalkDirs --> MatchGitignoreDir{Gitignore match?}
        MatchGitignoreDir -- Yes --> PruneDir[Add to excluded dirs]
        MatchGitignoreDir -- No --> MatchExcludeDir{Exclude pattern match?}
        MatchExcludeDir -- Yes --> PruneDir
        MatchExcludeDir -- No --> KeepDir[Keep directory in traversal]
    end

    subgraph FileFiltering[File Level Filter]
        KeepDir --> CheckGitignoreFile{Gitignore match?}
        CheckGitignoreFile -- Yes --> SkipFile[Skip file]
        CheckGitignoreFile -- No --> CheckExcludeFile{Exclude pattern match?}
        CheckExcludeFile -- Yes --> SkipFile
        CheckExcludeFile -- No --> CheckIncludeFile{Include pattern set and no match?}
        CheckIncludeFile -- Yes --> SkipFile
        CheckIncludeFile -- No --> CheckSize{Size > max_file_size?}
        CheckSize -- Yes --> SkipSize[Log Size Limit Skip]
        CheckSize -- No --> ReadContent[Read with utf-8-sig]
    end

    ReadContent --> TextCheck{Decode Success?}
    TextCheck -- Yes --> AddDict[Store in files_dict]
    TextCheck -- No --> SkipBin[Log Non-Text Skip]

    AddDict --> Summary[Print Summary Report]
    SkipFile --> Summary
    SkipSize --> Summary
    SkipBin --> Summary
    Summary --> End([Return dict])

docs.title: crawl_local_files()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: 

def crawl_local_files(
    directory,
    include_patterns=None,
    exclude_patterns=None,
    max_file_size=None,
    use_relative_paths=True,
):

Description: Traverses a target directory on the local filesystem, filters out ignored or irrelevant files/directories, reads matching text files, and compiles their contents into a dictionary.

The function operates through several distinct phases: 1. Validation & Initialization: Verifies that the provided path points to a valid directory. Initializes ANSI escape codes for terminal feedback, counters for tracking scan metrics, and the output dictionary. 2. Gitignore Parsing: Detects if a .gitignore file exists in the root of the target directory. If found, reads it using utf-8-sig encoding and compiles it into a pathspec.PathSpec object using the gitwildmatch rule style. 3. Directory Pruning: While walking through the directory hierarchy with os.walk, checks each directory against the gitignore rules and exclude_patterns. Any matched directory is removed in-place from dirs to prevent os.walk from descending into its children. 4. File Filtering & Extraction: Evaluates each file against the gitignore rules, exclude_patterns, include_patterns, and max_file_size constraints. 5. Text Decoding: Attempts to read each valid file using open(filepath, "r", encoding="utf-8-sig"). Non-text files or files that raise UnicodeDecodeError or ValueError are categorized as non-text and skipped without crashing the traversal process. 6. Summary Generation: Outputs ANSI-colorized summary metrics displaying total entries examined, successfully processed files, excluded paths, size limit violations, and non-text skips.

    if not os.path.isdir(directory):
        raise ValueError(f"Directory does not exist: {directory}")

    files_dict = {}

    # --- ANSI colors ---
    C_GREEN  = "\033[92m"
    C_GRAY   = "\033[90m"
    C_RED    = "\033[91m"
    C_RESET  = "\033[0m"

    # --- Counters ---
    entry_num = 0
    count_processed = 0
    count_excluded = 0
    count_size_limit = 0
    count_non_text = 0
    skipped_size_limit = []
    skipped_non_text = []

    # --- Load .gitignore ---
    gitignore_path = os.path.join(directory, ".gitignore")
    gitignore_spec = None
    if os.path.exists(gitignore_path):
        try:
            with open(gitignore_path, "r", encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
                gitignore_patterns = f.readlines()
            gitignore_spec = pathspec.PathSpec.from_lines("gitwildmatch", gitignore_patterns)
            print(f"Loaded .gitignore patterns from {gitignore_path}")
        except Exception as e:
            print(f"Warning: Could not read or parse .gitignore file {gitignore_path}: {e}")
    # ...

The initial block handles validation and .gitignore ingestion. If directory is invalid, a ValueError is raised immediately before any state is initialized. The .gitignore loader catches general exceptions gracefully to avoid failing the crawl when .gitignore files contain unreadable characters or permissions issues.

    # ...
    # --- Single-pass: walk, filter, and process inline ---
    for root, dirs, files in os.walk(directory):
        # --- Directory filtering ---
        excluded_dirs = set()
        for d in sorted(dirs):
            dirpath_rel = os.path.relpath(os.path.join(root, d), directory)

            reason = None
            if gitignore_spec and gitignore_spec.match_file(dirpath_rel):
                reason = "excluded (.gitignore)"
            elif exclude_patterns:
                for pattern in exclude_patterns:
                    dir_pattern = pattern[:-2] if pattern.endswith("/*") else pattern
                    if fnmatch.fnmatch(dirpath_rel, dir_pattern) or fnmatch.fnmatch(d, dir_pattern):
                        reason = "excluded"
                        break

            if reason:
                excluded_dirs.add(d)
                entry_num += 1
                count_excluded += 1
                print(f"{C_GRAY}  [{entry_num}] {dirpath_rel}/ [{reason}]{C_RESET}")

        for d in dirs.copy():
            if d in excluded_dirs:
                dirs.remove(d)

        # Sort remaining dirs for consistent traversal order
        dirs.sort()
        # ...

The directory filtering block prunes unneeded directory trees before recursing into them. Modifying dirs in-place by removing directories matching gitignore_spec or exclude_patterns prevents os.walk from traversing large subtrees (such as node_modules or .git), saving I/O overhead.

        # ...
        # --- File processing (inline, sorted) ---
        for filename in sorted(files):
            filepath = os.path.join(root, filename)
            relpath = os.path.relpath(filepath, directory) if use_relative_paths else filepath
            entry_num += 1

            # Check gitignore
            if gitignore_spec and gitignore_spec.match_file(relpath):
                count_excluded += 1
                print(f"{C_GRAY}  [{entry_num}] {relpath} [excluded (.gitignore)]{C_RESET}")
                continue

            # Check exclude patterns
            excluded = False
            if exclude_patterns:
                for pattern in exclude_patterns:
                    if fnmatch.fnmatch(relpath, pattern):
                        excluded = True
                        break
            if excluded:
                count_excluded += 1
                print(f"{C_GRAY}  [{entry_num}] {relpath} [excluded]{C_RESET}")
                continue

            # Check include patterns
            if include_patterns:
                matched = False
                for pattern in include_patterns:
                    if fnmatch.fnmatch(relpath, pattern):
                        matched = True
                        break
                if not matched:
                    count_excluded += 1
                    print(f"{C_GRAY}  [{entry_num}] {relpath} [excluded (not in include list)]{C_RESET}")
                    continue

            # Check size limit
            if max_file_size and os.path.getsize(filepath) > max_file_size:
                count_size_limit += 1
                skipped_size_limit.append(relpath)
                size_kb = os.path.getsize(filepath) / 1024
                print(f"{C_RED}  [{entry_num}] {relpath} [size limit: {size_kb:.0f}KB]{C_RESET}")
                continue

            # Try to read as text
            try:
                with open(filepath, "r", encoding="utf-8-sig") as f:
                    content = f.read()
                files_dict[relpath] = content
                count_processed += 1
                print(f"{C_GREEN}  [{entry_num}] {relpath} [processed]{C_RESET}")
            except (UnicodeDecodeError, ValueError):
                count_non_text += 1
                skipped_non_text.append(relpath)
                print(f"{C_RED}  [{entry_num}] {relpath} [cannot process: not a text file]{C_RESET}")
            except Exception as e:
                count_non_text += 1
                skipped_non_text.append(relpath)
                print(f"{C_RED}  [{entry_num}] {relpath} [cannot process: {e}]{C_RESET}")
    # ...

The file filtering logic evaluates files individually. If an include_patterns set is provided, files not matching any pattern in the set are excluded. Size limits are checked using os.path.getsize before opening the file. File reading is wrapped in broad exception handling to trap UnicodeDecodeError and other I/O errors, ensuring that binary files or unreadable nodes do not interrupt the crawl.

    # ...
    # --- Summary ---
    total_fetched = count_processed + count_excluded + count_size_limit + count_non_text
    print("\n--- Crawl Summary ---")
    print(f"  Total found : {total_fetched}")
    print(f"{C_GREEN}  Processed   : {count_processed}{C_RESET}")
    if count_excluded > 0:
        print(f"{C_GRAY}  Excluded    : {count_excluded}{C_RESET}")
    if count_size_limit > 0:
        print(f"{C_RED}  Size limit  : {count_size_limit}{C_RESET}")
        for f in skipped_size_limit:
            print(f"{C_RED}    - {f}{C_RESET}")
    if count_non_text > 0:
        print(f"{C_RED}  Non-text    : {count_non_text}{C_RESET}")
        for f in skipped_non_text:
            print(f"{C_RED}    - {f}{C_RESET}")
    print("---------------------")

    return {"files": files_dict}

The summary block formats crawl statistics into a consolidated report written to stdout. Lists of files skipped due to size limits or non-text decoding errors are printed in red ANSI text.

Parameters: * directory (str): The root path to the local directory to crawl. * include_patterns (set | None, optional): Set of file glob patterns to match against (e.g., {"*.py", "*.js"}). Defaults to None (includes all files not otherwise excluded). * exclude_patterns (set | None, optional): Set of file or directory glob patterns to ignore (e.g., {"tests/*", "*.pyc"}). Defaults to None. * max_file_size (int | None, optional): Maximum allowed file size in bytes. Files larger than this threshold are skipped. Defaults to None. * use_relative_paths (bool, optional): Whether the output dictionary keys should be relative to directory (True) or absolute/verbatim paths (False). Defaults to True.

Returns: * dict: A dictionary containing a single key "files", mapping file paths (relative or absolute) to their string text content ({"files": {filepath: content}}).

Raises: * ValueError: Raised if directory is not an existing directory according to os.path.isdir.

Example: 

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("--- Crawling parent directory ('..') ---")
    files_data = crawl_local_files(
        "..",
        exclude_patterns={
            "*.pyc",
            "__pycache__/*",
            ".venv/*",
            ".git/*",
            "docs/*",
            "output/*",
        },
    )
    print(f"Found {len(files_data['files'])} files:")
    for path in files_data["files"]:
        print(f"  {path}")

def build_code_file_filter_prompt(project_name: str, file_listing: str) -> str:

    Used in api-reference mode to identify which files are actual code modules

    """

        f"For the project `{project_name}`, here is the list of all files in the codebase:\n\n"
        f"{file_listing}\n\n"
        f"Your task is to identify WHICH of these files are ACTUAL CODE files that contain "

        f"EXCLUDE: UI layouts (like .xaml, .storyboard, .html), configuration files "
        f"(like .xml, .json, .manifest, .ini), static assets, build scripts "
        f"(like .csproj, .sln), and documentation.\n\n"
        f"Return ONLY a YAML list of the file indices that should be documented as code modules.\n\n"
        f"```yaml\n- 0\n- 1\n- 3\n```"
    )

By providing a strict exclusion list covering UI markups (.xaml, .storyboard, .html), configurations (.xml, .json, .manifest, .ini), build system definitions (.csproj, .sln), and standalone documentation, it minimizes token waste in subsequent generation passes. The return specification constrains the model response to a clean YAML sequence of numeric integer indices matching the provided listing, enabling deterministic parsing by regex or YAML loaders in upstream graph nodes such as nodes.

Description: Constructs a structured prompt instructing the LLM to summarize a newly generated documentation chapter. This summary is injected into future chapter prompts to provide running architectural context across iterative LLM invocations. The prompt guides the model to produce 3 to 5 sentences across four technical dimensions: component scope, key technical elements, implementation patterns, and system integration dependencies. It also supports localization by dynamically prefixing a language directive if a non-English language is specified.

Parameters: * chapter_num (int): The numerical index of the chapter being summarized. * abstraction_name (str): The title or high-level abstraction name of the chapter. * chapter_content (str): The raw Markdown text of the generated chapter. * language (str, optional): Target language for the summary output. Defaults to "english".

Returns: * str: A formatted prompt ready to be evaluated by the LLM summarizer.

Raises: * This function does not raise exceptions internally.

Example: 

def build_chapter_summary_prompt(chapter_num: int, abstraction_name: str,
                                  chapter_content: str, language: str = "english") -> str:
    """Build the prompt for generating a technical summary of a written chapter.

    Used after each chapter is generated to create a concise technical summary
    for cross-chapter context. The summary is fed into subsequent chapters'
    prompts so the LLM maintains coherence across the full document.
    """
    lang_instruction = (
        f"Write the entire summary in {language.capitalize()}. "
        if language.lower() != "english" else ""
    )
    return (
        f"{lang_instruction}"
        f"Summarize the following documentation chapter as a structured technical brief. "
        f"For EACH of the 4 points below, write 3-5 concise technical sentences:\n\n"
        f"(1) **Component Scope & Responsibility**: What is the main technical domain this "
        f"chapter covers? What problems does it solve and what role does it play in the system?\n\n"
        f"(2) **Key Technical Elements**: What are the specific classes, services, functions, "
        f"data models, or protocols discussed? Name them and describe their concrete roles.\n\n"
        f"(3) **Implementation Patterns & Architecture**: What design patterns, communication "
        f"protocols, data flow strategies, error handling mechanisms, or security measures "
        f"are covered? How are they implemented?\n\n"
        f"(4) **System Integration & Dependencies**: How does this component interface with "
        f"other parts of the system? What does it consume from or provide to other components? "
        f"What are the key integration points?\n\n"
        f"---\n"
        f"Chapter {chapter_num}: {abstraction_name}\n"
        f"{chapter_content}"
    )

The prompt built by build_chapter_summary_prompt enforces an information-dense format across four explicit technical dimensions, preventing the LLM from generating vague or superficial summaries. By segregating the evaluation into component scope, concrete elements, architectural design patterns, and cross-system integration points, the resulting summary captures critical interface boundaries and state models needed by subsequent chapter generation nodes. The helper conditionally prepends a language enforcement directive if language is not set to "english", ensuring multi-lingual documentation runs maintain consistent target language outputs across chapter briefs.

    - Material theme with code copy buttons
    - Syntax highlighting (pymdownx.highlight + inlinehilite)
    - Mermaid diagram rendering via pymdownx.superfences custom fences
    - Navigation from the generated nav_snippet
    """
    # Extract nav items from nav_snippet (strip the "nav:" header line)
    nav_lines = nav_yaml.split("\n")
    nav_body = "\n".join(nav_lines[1:]) if nav_lines else ""

    return (
        f"site_name: '{site_name}'\n"
        f"theme:\n"
        f"  name: material\n"
        f"  features:\n"
        f"    - content.code.copy\n"
        f"markdown_extensions:\n"
        f"  - pymdownx.highlight:\n"
        f"      anchor_linenums: true\n"
        f"      use_pygments: true\n"
        f"  - pymdownx.superfences:\n"
        f"      custom_fences:\n"
        f"        - name: mermaid\n"
        f"          class: mermaid\n"
        f"          format: !!python/name:pymdownx.superfences.fence_code_format\n"
        f"  - pymdownx.inlinehilite\n"
        f"nav:\n"
        f"  - Home: index.md\n"
        f"{nav_body}\n"
    )

build_mkdocs_config handles the transition between AI-generated navigation snippets and static site generator configuration files. When nav_yaml is passed in, the function splits the string by newlines and drops the first line (nav:) to avoid duplicate YAML keys, rejoining the remaining indented body underneath the base Home: index.md root item. The output configuration includes pymdownx.superfences custom fences mapped to !!python/name:pymdownx.superfences.fence_code_format, which allows browsers to dynamically render Mermaid sequence, flowchart, and class diagrams without requiring external precompilation tools.

docs.title: Technical Overview
docs.text:
The utils.token_utils module provides token measurement, estimation, and diagnostic logging utilities for LLM prompts across the pipeline. It manages a lazily initialized singleton tiktoken encoding model (cl100k_base) with a graceful character-heuristic fallback mechanism (len(text) // 4) if tokenizer initialization fails or if the environment lacks complete tokenizer resources.

Additionally, this module provides structured logging and ANSI-colored terminal analytics via log_token_estimation, giving real-time visibility into prompt token counts, prompt capacity utilization against configured maximums, and itemized breakdowns of dynamic prompt sections.

docs.title: _get_encoding()
docs.text:
Visibility: Private (Internal helper) Signature: def _get_encoding() -> tiktoken.Encoding | None:

Description: Implements a lazy-loading singleton pattern for the tiktoken tokenizer encoding. It checks the module-scoped _encoding variable, attempting to instantiate the standard OpenAI cl100k_base BPE tokenizer if not already loaded. If an exception occurs during initialization (e.g., missing tokenizer dictionary files or network/environment restrictions), the exception is suppressed and _encoding is set to None, ensuring that downstream token counting degrades safely to heuristic estimation without crashing the calling node.

Parameters: * None

Returns: * tiktoken.Encoding | None: The initialized cl100k_base encoding object if available; otherwise None.

Raises: * None (all internal exceptions from tiktoken.get_encoding are caught internally).

Example: 

def _get_encoding():
    global _encoding
    if _encoding is None:
        try:
            _encoding = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")
        except Exception:
            _encoding = None
    return _encoding

The function relies on global state mutation (global _encoding) to guarantee that the BPE vocabulary table is loaded at most once during the process lifecycle. The broad except Exception clause guarantees fault tolerance in offline or resource-constrained environments where binary token assets cannot be verified or downloaded. Once resolved, subsequent invocations bypass the initialization block entirely and return the cached reference.

docs.title: count_tokens()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def count_tokens(text: str) -> int:

Description: Calculates the number of tokens in a provided string. It first performs a fast check for empty or falsy strings, returning 0 immediately. If text is present, it retrieves the encoding instance from _get_encoding(). When an encoding object is active, it encodes the string using byte-pair encoding and returns the exact token list length. If the encoding object is unavailable, it calculates an integer division approximation (len(text) // 4), matching the standard four-characters-per-token heuristic for English text.

Parameters: * text (str): The raw text string or prompt content whose tokens need to be calculated.

Returns: * int: The exact or estimated token count. Returns 0 if text is empty or None.

Raises: * None

Example: 

def count_tokens(text: str) -> int:
    """Count tokens using tiktoken, with fallback to chars/4."""
    if not text:
        return 0
    enc = _get_encoding()
    if enc:
        return len(enc.encode(text))
    return len(text) // 4

This function acts as the unified token measurement interface for the application. By centralizing token calculation, prompt builders across utils.prompts and node executors in nodes can determine payload sizes prior to making network requests. The fallback calculation len(text) // 4 ensures pipeline continuity in development or testing environments where tiktoken native bindings or vocabularies might not be fully configured.

docs.title: log_token_estimation()
docs.text:
Visibility: Public Signature: def log_token_estimation(node_name: str, prompt_content: str, max_tokens: int, token_usage: dict | None = None) -> None:

Description: Measures prompt size, calculates capacity consumption relative to the configured context window limit, builds sub-component usage breakdowns, and emits formatted messages to both the standard console output and the structured file logger. Console output uses yellow ANSI escape sequences (\033[93m...\033[0m) for high visibility during live executions, while file logs write standardized NODE EXEC pipe-delimited log lines through llm_logger.

Parameters: * node_name (str): The name or identifier of the execution node invoking the LLM (e.g., node names defined in flow or nodes). * prompt_content (str): The full text string of the assembled prompt to be evaluated. * max_tokens (int): The maximum token capacity allocated for the model or node context. * token_usage (dict | None, optional): A key-value mapping of sub-component names to their respective token counts (e.g., {"system_prompt": 120, "context": 1500}). Defaults to None.

Returns: * None

Raises: * None

Example: 

def log_token_estimation(node_name: str, prompt_content: str, max_tokens: int,
                         token_usage: dict | None = None) -> None:
    token_count = count_tokens(prompt_content)
    percentage = (token_count / max_tokens) * 100 if max_tokens else 0

    # Build token usage string if provided
    usage_str = ""
    if token_usage:
        parts = []
        for label, value in token_usage.items():
            pct = (value / token_count * 100) if token_count else 0
            parts.append(f"{label}={value:,} ({pct:.0f}%)")
        usage_str = " | " + " | ".join(parts)

    # Console output (yellow) with token usage
    print(f"\033[93m[Token Analytics] {node_name}: {token_count:,} / {max_tokens:,} tokens ({percentage:.1f}% capacity){usage_str}\033[0m")

    # File log with node context and token usage
    logger.info(f"NODE EXEC | node={node_name} | prompt_tokens={token_count:,} / {max_tokens:,} ({percentage:.1f}% capacity){usage_str}")

The function computes the global token count of prompt_content using count_tokens(). It then computes the overall context consumption ratio percentage, guarding against division by zero when max_tokens is set to 0. If an optional token_usage dictionary is supplied, it iterates over each sub-section metric, formatting individual counts with comma separators and relative percentages against the total prompt token count. Finally, it formats dual outputs: an ANSI-colored string directly written to stdout via print(), and a structured record sent to logger.info().
